network.overall_strategy: This network is surface-centered and uses acetaldehyde as the main convergence hub. A compact cyanosulfidic photoredox module supplies acetaldehyde from acetonitrile, after which three target-relevant terrestrial families branch to threonine: (i) the best-defined lactonitrile-lactaldehyde-Strecker sequence, (ii) the independent aminomalononitrile plus acetaldehyde route, and (iii) the catalyst-free glycine plus acetaldehyde condensation. Free threonine is separated explicitly from aminonitrile or dinitrile precursors because the literature often demonstrates precursor formation or post-hydrolysis release rather than direct accumulation of free threonine. Hot hydrothermal synthesis is not prioritized because threonine is thermolabile at elevated hydrothermal temperatures, and unresolved ensemble routes such as spark, radiolysis, and ice chemistry are omitted here to keep the graph stoichiometrically explicit. The target node tracks threonine even though most experiments also co-produce allothreonine and racemates.

reactions.name: Cu(I)-assisted photoredox reduction of acetonitrile to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Near-neutral phosphate-buffered anoxic water under UV irradiation; H2S is the stoichiometric reductant and sulfur is represented as the net oxidized sulfur sink

reactions.mechanism: UV-excited Cu(I)/sulfide photoredox reduces the nitrile carbon to an imine-equivalent that hydrolyzes to the aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) demonstrated UV/H2S/Cu(I) photoredox conversion of HCN-derived nitriles to aldehydes, and Patel et al. (2015) placed acetaldehyde within the same cyanosulfidic homologation network. This node is written as a net nitrile-to-aldehyde transformation with explicit sulfur bookkeeping rather than as an unbalanced shorthand.

reactions.name: Cu-free photoredox reduction of acetonitrile to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Near-neutral anoxic water under UV irradiation with H2S reductant; Cu-free variant of the cyanosulfidic reduction module

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-driven photoredox reduces the nitrile carbon and hydrolysis reveals the aldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) indicate that Cu(I) is not an invariant requirement in all H2S-containing cyanosulfidic variants, and Xu et al. (2018) showed that alternative non-Cu photoredox systems can replace Cu(I) in HCN homologation. The exact acetonitrile-to-acetaldehyde Cu-free implementation is therefore weaker than rxn_001 but chemically justified.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous solution with elevated cyanide activity

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds nucleophilically to acetaldehyde and proton transfer yields the cyanohydrin lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Acetaldehyde plus HCN to give lactonitrile is the immediate cyanohydrin step preceding lactaldehyde formation in the Ritson-Sutherland route (Ritson and Sutherland, 2013). This is one of the most secure elementary edges in the threonine precursor sequence.

reactions.name: Cu(I)-assisted photoredox reduction of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde

conditions.other: Near-neutral phosphate-buffered anoxic water under UV irradiation; representative laboratory analog uses short-wave UV

reactions.mechanism: Photoredox reduction of the nitrile carbon followed by hydrolytic unmasking converts lactonitrile into lactaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) directly obtained lactaldehyde from the acetaldehyde-cyanohydrin system in 19% yield under UV/H2S/Cu(I)/phosphate conditions; Patel et al. (2015) embedded this step in a broader cyanosulfidic network. This is the strongest mechanistically resolved threonine-precursor edge in the literature.

reactions.name: Cu-free photoredox reduction of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde

conditions.other: Near-neutral anoxic water under UV irradiation with H2S reductant; Cu-free variant

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide-driven photoredox reduces the cyanohydrin nitrile and hydrolysis yields lactaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Cu-free H2S-driven variants of cyanosulfidic reduction are discussed by Patel et al. (2015), although the best threonine-specific lactaldehyde data are Cu-assisted. This alternative keeps explicit atom balance while acknowledging that the Cu-free implementation is less directly quantified for the threonine branch.

reactions.name: Strecker capture of lactaldehyde to threonine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Near-neutral to mildly basic anoxic water with HCN and excess NH3; formation can require days to weeks

reactions.mechanism: Lactaldehyde enters ordinary Strecker chemistry through imine/iminium and cyanide-addition steps to give the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Ritson and Sutherland (2013) explicitly showed that lactaldehyde, HCN, and excess NH3 give the threonine/allo-threonine Strecker aminonitrile. The precursor is experimentally much better supported than isolated free threonine, so it is retained as its own node.

reactions.name: Acid-promoted hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to threonine

conditions.other: Acidic geothermal pool or evaporitic surface film; multiple water equivalents are required and hydrolysis is kinetically slower than aminonitrile formation

reactions.mechanism: Stepwise nitrile hydration to amide and then carboxylic acid releases ammonia and yields threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Aminonitrile hydrolysis to amino acid is chemically standard, but the deep report emphasizes that many threonine studies relied on strong analytical hydrolysis rather than direct isolation of free threonine. This node is therefore a necessary but partially speculative environmental completion of the precursor route of Ritson and Sutherland (2013), with the hydrolysis caveat also relevant to Thanassi (1975).

reactions.name: HCN trimerization to aminomalononitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic concentrated cyanide in alkaline or evaporitically concentrated surface waters

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide oligomerization furnishes aminomalononitrile as the HCN trimer.
reactions.reasoning: Thanassi (1975) identifies aminomalononitrile as the HCN trimer used in the direct threonine route. Because cyanide concentration is the major geochemical bottleneck, evaporitically concentrated alkaline-lake settings are the most defensible terrestrial context (Toner and Catling, 2019).

reactions.name: Addition of aminomalononitrile to acetaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: The activated carbon of aminomalononitrile forms a new C-C bond to acetaldehyde, giving a beta-hydroxyl dinitrile adduct.
reactions.reasoning: Thanassi (1975) demonstrated the key C-C bond-forming reaction of aminomalononitrile with acetaldehyde under mild aqueous conditions, and Kuroda et al. (2020) explicitly discuss the same threonine-precursor logic. No mineral catalyst is required.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the aminomalononitrile-acetaldehyde adduct in acidic surface pools

conditions.other: Acidic aqueous workup analog in volcanic hot-spring or evaporitic settings; multiple water equivalents are required

reactions.mechanism: Both nitriles hydrolyze to carboxyl groups and the resulting aminomalonic acid derivative decarboxylates to threonine with release of ammonia and CO2.
reactions.reasoning: Thanassi (1975) obtained D,L-threonine and allo-threonine after hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the aminomalononitrile-acetaldehyde adduct, and Kuroda et al. (2020) summarize the same route. The C-C addition is experimentally strong, whereas natural equivalents of the laboratory acid workup remain less certain.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis and decarboxylation of the aminomalononitrile-acetaldehyde adduct during evaporitic wet-dry cycling

conditions.other: Repeated concentration and rehydration in acidic to mildly acidic surface films; lower-temperature alternative to rxn_010

reactions.mechanism: Concentration-driven hydration of the dinitrile followed by decarboxylation releases threonine, ammonia, and CO2.
reactions.reasoning: This is an alternative environmental realization of the same Thanassi-derived adduct-hydrolysis chemistry. The underlying threonine release is supported by Thanassi (1975), but mapping the laboratory hydrolysis onto natural wet-dry cycling is more speculative than the C-C addition itself.

reactions.name: Catalyst-free condensation of glycine with acetaldehyde to threonine

conditions.other: Homogeneous weakly acidic solution at pH 3.3-3.7; no inorganic solids; anoxic

reactions.mechanism: Nonenzymatic aldehyde-amino-acid C-C bond formation produces the threonine skeleton; the net step is the reverse of threonine retro-aldol cleavage.
reactions.reasoning: Ivanov and Ivanov (1983) reported threonine among products from glycine or glycine oligomers with acetaldehyde at pH 3.3-3.7 and 60-80 C, explicitly without inorganic solids. The route is experimentally direct but poorly selective and is expected to co-produce allothreonine and other amino acids.

pathways.name: Cu/Cu cyanosulfidic sequence
pathways.description: Cu-assisted upstream acetaldehyde supply and Cu-assisted lactonitrile reduction feed the best-defined lactaldehyde-Strecker branch to threonine.

pathways.name: Cu-upstream, Cu-free midstream cyanosulfidic sequence
pathways.description: Cu-assisted acetaldehyde supply is combined with a Cu-free lactonitrile-to-lactaldehyde photoreduction before Strecker capture and hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Cu-free upstream, Cu midstream cyanosulfidic sequence
pathways.description: Cu-free acetaldehyde supply is combined with Cu-assisted lactonitrile reduction and the standard lactaldehyde-Strecker completion.

pathways.name: Fully Cu-free cyanosulfidic sequence
pathways.description: Both nitrile-to-aldehyde photoreductions proceed without Cu, then lactaldehyde is trapped as the threonine aminonitrile and hydrolyzed.

pathways.name: AMN route with Cu acetaldehyde supply and hot-pool hydrolysis
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde from the Cu-assisted photoredox module reacts with aminomalononitrile and the adduct is hydrolyzed and decarboxylated in acidic surface pools.

pathways.name: AMN route with Cu acetaldehyde supply and wet-dry hydrolysis
pathways.description: The same aminomalononitrile addition chemistry is completed by a lower-temperature evaporitic wet-dry realization of hydrolysis and decarboxylation.

pathways.name: AMN route with Cu-free acetaldehyde supply and hot-pool hydrolysis
pathways.description: A Cu-free upstream acetaldehyde module feeds the aminomalononitrile branch, followed by acidic hydrolysis and decarboxylation.

pathways.name: AMN route with Cu-free acetaldehyde supply and wet-dry hydrolysis
pathways.description: A Cu-free acetaldehyde source is combined with the aminomalononitrile adduct route and completed by evaporitic cycling.

pathways.name: Direct glycine condensation using Cu acetaldehyde supply
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde from the Cu-assisted upstream module condenses directly with glycine under warm acidic aqueous conditions to give threonine.

pathways.name: Direct glycine condensation using Cu-free acetaldehyde supply
pathways.description: The same Ivanov-type glycine condensation is reached from the Cu-free acetaldehyde-supply variant.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest pathway in the network. The Cu(I)/H2S photoredox reductions, cyanohydrin formation, and lactaldehyde-to-aminonitrile Strecker chemistry are all well aligned with the cited threonine literature, but release of free threonine from the aminonitrile remains the least secure step under realistic surface conditions. rxn_007 is chemically plausible but needs a more explicit acidic hydrolysis context and one additional water in the stoichiometry.
suggestions: Specify UV, near-neutral pH, phosphate, and Cu(I)/CuCN availability for rxn_001 and rxn_004.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_010 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_011 + mol_002, or split aminonitrile hydrolysis into amide and acid substeps.
Consider adding allothreonine aminonitrile and allothreonine coproduct nodes to reflect the observed diastereomeric mixture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This hybrid route is plausible, but the Cu-free reduction of lactonitrile to lactaldehyde is less directly demonstrated than the Cu-assisted version. The pathway remains literature-aligned overall, yet the final aminonitrile hydrolysis still needs explicit acidic conditions and corrected stoichiometry.
suggestions: Provide explicit experimental support for Cu-free lactonitrile reduction, or keep the Cu-assisted midstream step in the conservative core network.
State the UV, sulfide, pH, and buffering conditions supporting rxn_005.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_010 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_011 + mol_002 and justify the hydrolysis environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This hybrid route benefits from the well-supported Cu-assisted lactonitrile reduction, but the upstream Cu-free acetonitrile-to-acetaldehyde step is only indirectly anchored by broader Cu-optional cyanosulfidic chemistry. The downstream hydrolysis to free threonine remains the main weakness.
suggestions: Provide direct support for Cu-free acetonitrile reduction, or keep the Cu-assisted upstream step in the core network.
Specify UV, pH, phosphate, and Cu availability for rxn_004.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_010 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_011 + mol_002 and give a realistic acidic hydrolysis setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Chemically possible, but this is the weakest cyanosulfidic variant because both photoredox reductions are Cu-free. The literature supports Cu-optional homologation in some contexts, but not this fully Cu-free threonine-specific sequence as strongly as the Cu-assisted branch, and aminonitrile hydrolysis is still underdefined.
suggestions: Either supply literature support for both Cu-free reductions or mark this pathway as speculative rather than core.
Consider replacing the generic Cu-free claim with a specific alternative photoredox module if that is the intended chemistry.
Rewrite rxn_007 as mol_010 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_011 + mol_002 and specify the hydrolysis conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The aminomalononitrile branch is a real independent threonine route and aligns well with the literature. Its weak point is the final hydrolysis/decarboxylation node, which compresses a multistep dinitrile-to-amino-acid conversion that likely needs stronger or longer-lived acidic conditions than a generic surface pool implies; rxn_008 and rxn_010 also need explicit stoichiometric coefficients.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_008 as 3 mol_001 -> mol_012.
Rewrite rxn_010 as mol_013 + 4 mol_003 -> mol_011 + 2 mol_002 + mol_015, or split it into hydrolysis and decarboxylation substeps.
Specify the acidity, temperature, and concentration mechanism required for AMN formation and downstream hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the best aminomalononitrile variant in the set. Wet-dry cycling makes concentration and persistence of reactive intermediates more credible, but the hydrolysis/decarboxylation remains a lumped, condition-sensitive transformation and rxn_011 is stoichiometrically incomplete as written.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_008 as 3 mol_001 -> mol_012.
Rewrite rxn_011 as mol_013 + 4 mol_003 -> mol_011 + 2 mol_002 + mol_015, or split it into hydrolysis and decarboxylation substeps.
Make the wet-dry acidity and temperature range explicit so the environmental basis for hydrolysis is clearer.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway keeps the valid AMN logic, but it is weakened by the less directly supported Cu-free acetaldehyde supply and by an over-compressed hot-pool hydrolysis/decarboxylation step. As written, the last node reads more like a laboratory workup summary than a well-specified environmental reaction.
suggestions: Provide direct support for Cu-free acetonitrile reduction, or replace rxn_002 with rxn_001 in the core version.
Rewrite rxn_008 as 3 mol_001 -> mol_012.
Rewrite rxn_010 as mol_013 + 4 mol_003 -> mol_011 + 2 mol_002 + mol_015 and specify realistic acidity and temperature.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Wet-dry cycling improves concentration realism relative to the hot-pool variant, but this route still depends on the less secure Cu-free acetaldehyde supply and on a lumped hydrolysis/decarboxylation step. The chemistry is plausible, but not as firmly grounded as the Cu-assisted or better specified alternatives.
suggestions: Provide direct support for Cu-free acetonitrile reduction, or keep the Cu-assisted upstream module in the conservative network.
Rewrite rxn_008 as 3 mol_001 -> mol_012.
Rewrite rxn_011 as mol_013 + 4 mol_003 -> mol_011 + 2 mol_002 + mol_015 and specify the acidic wet phase driving hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This route is directly aligned with the Ivanov glycine plus acetaldehyde chemistry and honestly targets free threonine rather than only an aminonitrile precursor. The main simplification is that rxn_012 compresses a known low-selectivity reaction network into a single clean edge and omits the experimentally important weakly acidic, warm aqueous conditions.
suggestions: Annotate rxn_012 with the known pH 3.3-3.7 and 60-80 C conditions.
Add allothreonine and broader amino-acid coproducts, or state explicitly that rxn_012 is a net edge over a mixed product ensemble.
Justify transport from the photoredox acetaldehyde source to the warm acidic condensation setting if these are distinct surface niches.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The direct condensation step itself is experimentally supported, but combining it with the less directly evidenced Cu-free acetaldehyde-supply step lowers confidence. The pathway also needs explicit warm acidic surface conditions for rxn_012 and does not capture the reaction's broad product spectrum.
suggestions: Provide direct support for the Cu-free upstream acetaldehyde supply, or replace rxn_002 with rxn_001 in the core pathway.
Annotate rxn_012 with pH 3.3-3.7 and 60-80 C.
Add allothreonine/coproduct nodes or mark rxn_012 as a low-selectivity net transformation.

evaluation.network_feedback: Network validity is high: 15 molecules and 12 reactions form a single connected graph with consistent IDs, and the RDKit check reports 0 UNBALANCED reactions. Literature alignment is also strong because the network captures the three best-supported threonine families from the supplied research and explicitly separates precursor-level formation from free-threonine release. The main weaknesses are environmental under-specification, because a generic Surface label is carrying distinct UV/Cu(I)/H2S near-neutral photoredox chemistry, near-neutral AMN addition chemistry, and weakly acidic to strongly acidic warm hydrolysis/condensation settings, plus weaker direct support for the Cu-free photoredox variants and overly lumped target-release steps. Four reactions need explicit stoichiometric correction even though they are balanceable: rxn_007 should be mol_010 + 2 mol_003 -> mol_011 + mol_002; rxn_008 should be 3 mol_001 -> mol_012; rxn_010 and rxn_011 should be mol_013 + 4 mol_003 -> mol_011 + 2 mol_002 + mol_015. Minor abstraction remains in collapsing experimentally common threonine/allothreonine and racemic mixtures into single target nodes. Overall, this is a good and chemically plausible network, but it is not approval-grade because the hydrolysis realism and environmental specification are still too coarse.
